content.text: Programs as Tools for Understanding Data

Raw data on its own tells us very little. Programs can be used to process data to acquire information — turning large collections of numbers, text, or records into meaningful insights and knowledge. This is one of the most powerful capabilities of computing: the ability to analyze data at a scale impossible for humans to do manually.

Programs can search, filter, transform, combine, compare, and visualize data sets to discover information and create new knowledge. Different tools are appropriate for different tasks — the key is knowing which process to apply to answer a given question.
Four Ways to Extract or Modify Data Using a Program

content.term: Four Ways to Extract or Modify Data Using a Program
content.definition:
1. Transforming — applying an operation to every element (e.g. doubling every number in a list)
2. Filtering — keeping only elements that meet a condition (e.g. keeping only positive numbers)
3. Combining or comparing — such as adding up a list or finding the highest value
4. Visualizing — representing a data set through a chart, graph, or other visual

rows: Transforming
Applies an operation to every element in the data set
Doubling every value in a list of revenue figures to project doubled sales; converting all temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit
Filtering
Keeps only the elements that meet a specified condition, removing everything else
Keeping only students with a GPA above 3.5 from a student records database; keeping only transactions above $1,000
Combining or comparing
Combines multiple values or compares values to find relationships or summaries
Adding up all sales figures to find total revenue; finding the student with the highest GPA; calculating the average temperature
Visualizing
Represents the data through a chart, graph, diagram, or other visual format
Creating a bar chart of monthly sales; a line graph of temperature over time; a map showing where users are located

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Know all four processes and be able to identify which one is being used in a scenario. Filtering = keeping only what meets a condition. Transforming = applying an operation to every element. Combining/comparing = finding a summary or comparing values. Visualizing = making a chart or graph.

content.definition: Search tools efficiently find information. Data filtering systems find information and recognize patterns. Spreadsheets help organize and find trends. Tables, diagrams, and visual tools communicate insight and knowledge gained from data.

rows: Search tools
Efficiently finding specific information within large data sets
Searching a database for all students with last name 'Smith'
Data filtering systems
Finding information that meets specific criteria and recognizing patterns in data
Filtering sales records to find all orders from a specific region
Spreadsheets
Organizing data into rows and columns, calculating totals, finding trends
Tracking monthly expenses and calculating yearly totals with automatic formulas
Tables, diagrams, visual tools
Communicating insight and knowledge gained from data to other people
A pie chart showing market share, a line graph showing growth over time

content.text: Using Programs Iteratively to Gain Insight

content.term: How do programs gain insight from data?
content.definition: Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way. Programmers can filter, clean, combine, cluster, classify, and transform data. Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs.

content.term: What does it mean to process data iteratively?
content.definition: Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way — meaning the programmer runs the program, examines the output, refines the approach, and runs it again. This cycle allows users to gradually gain deeper insight and knowledge from the data.

content.text: The iterative process of working with data looks like this: a programmer writes a program to process a data set, runs it, examines the results, notices something interesting or unexpected, refines the program to investigate further, and runs it again. Each cycle reveals more about the data.

rows: First run
Calculate average test score across all students
Average is 74 — lower than expected
Second run
Filter by grade level and calculate average for each
9th graders average 68; 12th graders average 82 — a significant gap
Third run
Filter by both grade level and school district
The gap is larger in certain districts — possibly related to resources
Fourth run
Combine with school funding data and compare
Schools with lower per-student funding show larger grade-level gaps — a pattern emerges

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs. A single run of a program may not reveal the most interesting insight — the iterative process of refining the analysis is what allows deeper knowledge to be extracted from data.
Combining data sources, clustering data, and classifying data are all parts of the process of using programs to gain insight and knowledge from data.

rows: Combining data sources
Merging data from multiple sources into one data set for analysis
Combining sales data, customer location data, and weather data to understand how weather affects purchasing
Clustering data
Grouping data points that are similar to each other into clusters
Grouping customers by purchasing behavior to identify distinct customer types for targeted marketing
Classifying data
Assigning data points to predefined categories based on their characteristics
Classifying emails as spam or not spam based on their content and sender

content.text: Insight and knowledge can also be obtained from translating and transforming digitally represented information. For example, translating text from one language to another, converting audio to text, or transforming raw sensor data into human-readable measurements are all ways programs create new knowledge from existing data.
Putting It Together: A Full Data Analysis Example
A city government wants to reduce traffic congestion. Here is how a programmer might use programs with data to gain insight:

items: COMBINE: Merge traffic camera data, GPS speed data, and public transit ridership data into one data set
FILTER: Keep only data from peak hours (7–9 AM and 4–7 PM) when congestion is worst
TRANSFORM: Convert raw vehicle counts into congestion index scores for each intersection
COMPARE: Find the top 10 most congested intersections during peak hours
VISUALIZE: Create a heat map of the city showing congestion levels at different times
ITERATE: Notice that congestion spikes on rainy days → add weather data → discover that bus ridership drops 30% on rainy days, increasing car traffic

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: No single step above would reveal the weather-congestion connection on its own. It is the iterative, multi-step process of combining, filtering, transforming, and analyzing that allows meaningful patterns to emerge from the data.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: Programs can process data to acquire information

Four ways to extract or modify data: transforming (apply to every element), filtering (keep only what meets a condition), combining or comparing (find summaries or relationships), visualizing (create charts/graphs)
Search tools find information efficiently; filtering systems find patterns; spreadsheets organize and find trends; visual tools communicate insights
Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way — run, examine, refine, repeat
Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs
Combining data sources, clustering data, and classifying data are parts of gaining insight from data
Insight can be obtained from translating and transforming digitally represented information
